# Invite lifecycle: email delivery, CSV export, and seven-day expiry

Label: needs-triage

## Problem Statement

The guestlist service can create and retain an invite, but invitees are not notified, operators cannot export invite data, and invites have no defined expiration behavior. This leaves invite delivery manual, makes downstream guest-list workflows difficult, and allows stale invitations to remain active indefinitely.

## Solution

Extend the invite lifecycle so that creating an invite sends an email through the existing notifier, all invite data can be exported as a standards-compatible CSV, and an invite is active only through seven days after its creation timestamp. Expiration must be evaluated using the service clock so behavior is deterministic and testable.

## User Stories

1. As an event organizer, I want an email sent when I create an invite, so that the guest receives the invitation immediately.
2. As an event organizer, I want the email sent to the invite’s email address, so that delivery is associated with the correct guest.
3. As an event organizer, I want the invitation email to have a clear subject and useful body, so that the guest understands why they received it and what to do next.
4. As an event organizer, I want invite creation to retain the existing name, email, phone, and creation timestamp, so that the guest list remains available after notification.
5. As an event organizer, I want the invite creation operation to use the configured notification transport, so that production transports and recording test transports behave consistently.
6. As an event organizer, I want every stored invite represented in an export, so that I can use the complete guest-list data elsewhere.
7. As an event organizer, I want the export to be CSV, so that it can be opened by spreadsheet tools and processed by other systems.
8. As an event organizer, I want the CSV to include a header row, so that each exported value is unambiguous.
9. As an event organizer, I want the CSV to include each invite’s name, email, phone, and creation timestamp, so that no invite data is lost during export.
10. As an event organizer, I want CSV values to be escaped according to CSV rules, so that commas, quotes, and line breaks in guest data do not corrupt the export.
11. As an event organizer, I want an invite to expire seven days after creation, so that old invitations cannot remain active forever.
12. As an event organizer, I want the seven-day period calculated from the invite’s creation timestamp, so that expiration is consistent regardless of when the invite is checked.
13. As an event organizer, I want expiration checks to use the service’s clock, so that behavior is deterministic in tests and consistent with the application’s time source.
14. As an event organizer, I want an invite to remain active before the seven-day boundary, so that a guest can use a valid invitation during the full allowed period.
15. As an event organizer, I want an invite to be expired at the seven-day boundary and afterward, so that the expiration rule has a precise, predictable cutoff.
16. As an event organizer, I want expired invites distinguishable from active invites, so that downstream guest-list workflows can exclude stale invitations.
17. As an event organizer, I want exporting invite data to include expired invites, so that the export remains a complete historical record of created invites.
18. As a maintainer, I want notification, export, and expiration behavior isolated behind small interfaces, so that each concern can be tested independently.
19. As a maintainer, I want existing invite storage behavior preserved, so that current consumers do not lose access to created invites.
20. As a maintainer, I want notification and expiration edge cases covered by tests, so that future changes do not silently break the invite lifecycle.

## Implementation Decisions

- Extend the invite domain model with the minimum lifecycle information needed to determine whether an invite is active or expired; retain the creation timestamp as the source of truth.
- Keep invite creation as the orchestration boundary: create and store the invite, then call the configured notifier’s email method for the new invite.
- Define a stable invitation email subject and body contract, with the invitee email as the recipient. The notifier remains responsible for transport delivery.
- Add a focused CSV export capability that serializes all stored invites with a header and the fields name, email, phone, and created timestamp.
- Use the standard library CSV behavior so values are correctly quoted and escaped.
- Add an expiration query or status capability on the invite service/domain. An invite is active when the current service time is earlier than its creation time plus seven calendar days; it is expired at or after that boundary.
- Inject the clock into all time-dependent behavior, preserving deterministic tests and avoiding direct wall-clock calls in lifecycle logic.
- Keep expired invites in storage and in exports; expiration changes their status, not their historical existence.
- Do not add SMS delivery to creation as part of this change; the requested automatic notification is email only.

## Testing Decisions

- Test external behavior through the public invite service and notifier recording behavior rather than implementation details.
- Add a creation test asserting that one email is sent to the invite email address with the agreed subject/body contract.
- Add tests proving the invite remains active before seven days, expires exactly at seven days, and remains expired afterward, using an injected fixed clock.
- Add tests proving export contains the header and every invite, including expired invites.
- Add CSV escaping coverage for names or contact values containing commas, quotes, and line breaks.
- Preserve the existing storage, display-name, and pricing tests.
- Test isolated export and expiration helpers where they expose stable domain behavior; avoid tests coupled to private data structures or formatting implementation beyond the CSV contract.

## Out of Scope

- Implementing real email provider credentials, delivery retries, bounce handling, or email templates beyond the service’s subject/body contract.
- Adding invitation links, RSVP tracking, acceptance/rejection states, authentication, or access control.
- Sending SMS automatically when an invite is created.
- Deleting expired invites or automatically purging exported history.
- Building a user interface, file-download endpoint, scheduler, or background job.
- Changing pricing or display-name behavior.

## Further Notes

The current codebase already provides a notifier abstraction and a recording notifier suitable for lifecycle tests. The implementation should preserve those seams. The seven-day rule should be documented as a precise duration boundary: an invite created at time T is active before T + 7 days and expired at T + 7 days.

# Invite lifecycle: SMS delivery, seven-day expiry, and Arabic guest names

Label: needs-triage

## Problem Statement

The guestlist service can create and retain an invite, but invitees are not notified, invites have no defined expiration behavior, and Arabic guest names can be rendered as blank. This leaves invite delivery manual, allows stale invitations to remain active indefinitely, and makes the guest list unusable for affected names.

## Solution

Extend the invite lifecycle so that creating an invite sends an SMS through the existing notifier, an invite is active only through seven days after its creation timestamp, and guest-name display preserves Arabic text and never renders a blank result for a non-empty Arabic name. CSV export is explicitly cancelled and must not be added.

## User Stories

1. As an event organizer, I want an SMS sent when I create an invite, so that the guest receives the invitation immediately.
2. As an event organizer, I want the SMS sent to the invite’s phone number, so that delivery is associated with the correct guest.
3. As an event organizer, I want the invitation SMS to have a clear message, so that the guest understands why they received it and what to do next.
4. As an event organizer, I want invite creation to retain the existing name, email, phone, and creation timestamp, so that the guest list remains available after notification.
5. As an event organizer, I want the invite creation operation to use the configured SMS notification transport, so that production transports and recording test transports behave consistently.
6. As an event organizer, I want an invite to expire seven days after creation, so that old invitations cannot remain active forever.
7. As an event organizer, I want the seven-day period calculated from the invite’s creation timestamp, so that expiration is consistent regardless of when the invite is checked.
8. As an event organizer, I want expiration checks to use the service’s clock, so that behavior is deterministic in tests and consistent with the application’s time source.
9. As an event organizer, I want an invite to remain active before seven days, so that a guest can use a valid invitation during the full allowed period.
10. As an event organizer, I want an invite to be expired at the seven-day boundary and afterward, so that the expiration rule has a precise, predictable cutoff.
11. As an event organizer, I want expired invites distinguishable from active invites, so that downstream guest-list workflows can exclude stale invitations.
12. As an event organizer, I want Arabic guest names displayed as readable Arabic text, so that the guest list works for Arabic-speaking guests.
13. As an event organizer, I want a non-empty Arabic name never rendered as a blank label, so that every named guest remains identifiable.
14. As an event organizer, I want blank or whitespace-only names handled with a non-empty fallback label, so that the guest list does not contain empty rows.
15. As an event organizer, I want Latin display-name title casing preserved, so that the correction does not regress existing guest-list presentation.
16. As a maintainer, I want notification, expiration, and display-name behavior isolated behind small interfaces, so that each concern can be tested independently.
17. As a maintainer, I want existing invite storage behavior preserved, so that current consumers do not lose access to created invites.
18. As a maintainer, I want SMS, expiration, and multilingual name edge cases covered by tests, so that future changes do not silently break the invite lifecycle.

## Implementation Decisions

- Keep invite creation as the orchestration boundary: create and store the invite, then call the configured notifier’s SMS method for the new invite.
- Define a stable invitation SMS message contract, with the invite phone number as the recipient. The notifier remains responsible for transport delivery.
- Add an expiration query or status capability on the invite service/domain. An invite is active when the current service time is earlier than its creation time plus seven days; it is expired at or after that boundary.
- Inject the clock into all time-dependent behavior, preserving deterministic tests and avoiding direct wall-clock calls in lifecycle logic.
- Keep expired invites in storage; expiration changes their status, not their historical existence.
- Correct display-name processing so Unicode, including Arabic characters, is preserved rather than converting all output through ASCII-only decoding.
- Apply the display-name length limit without splitting Unicode characters, and apply title casing only where it is appropriate for the text.
- Return a stable non-empty fallback such as `Guest` for blank or whitespace-only names. A non-empty Arabic name must remain non-empty and readable after formatting.
- Do not implement, retain, or expose CSV export as part of this work; the earlier CSV request is cancelled.
- Do not add email delivery; legal requires SMS only.

## Testing Decisions

- Test external behavior through the public invite service, display-name function, and recording notifier rather than implementation details.
- Add a creation test asserting that one SMS is sent to the invite phone number with the agreed message contract, and that no email is sent for creation.
- Add tests proving the invite remains active before seven days, expires exactly at seven days, and remains expired afterward, using an injected fixed clock.
- Add display-name tests for Arabic text, Arabic text at the length boundary, blank names, whitespace-only names, and existing Latin title casing.
- Preserve the existing invite-storage, display-name, and pricing tests, updating the display-name expectations where the corrected Unicode behavior changes them.
- Avoid tests for CSV generation because CSV export is out of scope and cancelled.

## Out of Scope

- Email delivery of any kind.
- CSV export, CSV formatting, or invite-data download.
- Real SMS provider credentials, delivery retries, bounce handling, or scheduling.
- Adding invitation links, RSVP tracking, acceptance/rejection states, authentication, or access control.
- Deleting expired invites or automatically purging invite history.
- Building a user interface, file-download endpoint, scheduler, or background job.
- Changing pricing behavior.

## Further Notes

The current codebase already provides a notifier abstraction with SMS and email methods, plus a recording notifier suitable for lifecycle tests. The implementation should preserve that seam while selecting SMS only. The seven-day rule is precise: an invite created at time T is active before T + 7 days and expired at T + 7 days. The current display-name implementation strips non-ASCII characters, which explains the blank Arabic output and should be replaced with Unicode-safe handling.

# Invite lifecycle: SMS delivery, 30-day expiry, restricted CSV, and Arabic guest names

Label: needs-triage

## Problem Statement

The guestlist service can create and retain an invite, but invitees are not notified, invites have no defined expiration behavior, Arabic guest names can be rendered as blank, and Finance lacks a safe export containing only the fields it needs.

## Solution

Extend the invite lifecycle so that creating an invite sends an SMS through the existing notifier, an invite is active for 30 days after its creation timestamp, guest-name display preserves Arabic text and never renders a blank result for a non-empty Arabic name, and Finance can export CSV containing only guest name and phone. Email delivery remains prohibited.

## User Stories

1. As an event organizer, I want an SMS sent when I create an invite, so that the guest receives the invitation immediately.
2. As an event organizer, I want the SMS sent to the invite’s phone number, so that delivery is associated with the correct guest.
3. As an event organizer, I want the invitation SMS to have a clear message, so that the guest understands why they received it and what to do next.
4. As an event organizer, I want invite creation to retain the existing name, email, phone, and creation timestamp, so that the guest list remains available after notification.
5. As an event organizer, I want the invite creation operation to use the configured SMS notification transport, so that production transports and recording test transports behave consistently.
6. As an event organizer, I want an invite to expire 30 days after creation, so that old invitations cannot remain active forever while guests have adequate time to respond.
7. As an event organizer, I want the 30-day period calculated from the invite’s creation timestamp, so that expiration is consistent regardless of when the invite is checked.
8. As an event organizer, I want expiration checks to use the service’s clock, so that behavior is deterministic in tests and consistent with the application’s time source.
9. As an event organizer, I want an invite to remain active before 30 days, so that a guest can use a valid invitation during the full allowed period.
10. As an event organizer, I want an invite to be expired at the 30-day boundary and afterward, so that the expiration rule has a precise, predictable cutoff.
11. As an event organizer, I want expired invites distinguishable from active invites, so that downstream guest-list workflows can exclude stale invitations.
12. As a Finance user, I want to export invite records as CSV, so that I can use guest contact data in finance workflows.
13. As a Finance user, I want the CSV to contain only name and phone, so that the export follows data-minimization requirements and does not expose email or timestamps.
14. As a Finance user, I want a CSV header identifying name and phone, so that the two exported fields are unambiguous.
15. As a Finance user, I want CSV values escaped correctly, so that commas, quotes, and line breaks in guest data do not corrupt the export.
16. As an event organizer, I want Arabic guest names displayed as readable Arabic text, so that the guest list works for Arabic-speaking guests.
17. As an event organizer, I want a non-empty Arabic name never rendered as a blank label, so that every named guest remains identifiable.
18. As an event organizer, I want blank or whitespace-only names handled with a non-empty fallback label, so that the guest list does not contain empty rows.
19. As an event organizer, I want Latin display-name title casing preserved, so that the correction does not regress existing guest-list presentation.
20. As a maintainer, I want notification, expiration, export, and display-name behavior isolated behind small interfaces, so that each concern can be tested independently.
21. As a maintainer, I want existing invite storage behavior preserved, so that current consumers do not lose access to created invites.
22. As a maintainer, I want SMS, expiration, restricted-export, and multilingual name edge cases covered by tests, so that future changes do not silently break the invite lifecycle.

## Implementation Decisions

- Keep invite creation as the orchestration boundary: create and store the invite, then call the configured notifier’s SMS method for the new invite.
- Define a stable invitation SMS message contract, with the invite phone number as the recipient. The notifier remains responsible for transport delivery.
- Add an expiration query or status capability on the invite service/domain. An invite is active when the current service time is earlier than its creation time plus 30 days; it is expired at or after that boundary.
- Inject the clock into all time-dependent behavior, preserving deterministic tests and avoiding direct wall-clock calls in lifecycle logic.
- Keep expired invites in storage; expiration changes their status, not their historical existence.
- Add a focused CSV export capability that serializes all stored invites as exactly two columns: name and phone, with a header row and no email, creation timestamp, or other invite fields.
- Use standard-library CSV behavior so values are correctly quoted and escaped.
- Correct display-name processing so Unicode, including Arabic characters, is preserved rather than converting all output through ASCII-only decoding.
- Apply the display-name length limit without splitting Unicode characters, and apply title casing only where it is appropriate for the text.
- Return a stable non-empty fallback such as `Guest` for blank or whitespace-only names. A non-empty Arabic name must remain non-empty and readable after formatting.
- Do not add email delivery; legal requires SMS only.

## Testing Decisions

- Test external behavior through the public invite service, export capability, display-name function, and recording notifier rather than implementation details.
- Add a creation test asserting that one SMS is sent to the invite phone number with the agreed message contract, and that no email is sent for creation.
- Add tests proving the invite remains active before 30 days, expires exactly at 30 days, and remains expired afterward, using an injected fixed clock.
- Add export tests proving the CSV has the expected name/phone header, includes all invites, excludes email and timestamps, and correctly escapes special values.
- Add display-name tests for Arabic text, Arabic text at the length boundary, blank names, whitespace-only names, and existing Latin title casing.
- Preserve the existing invite-storage, display-name, and pricing tests, updating display-name expectations where corrected Unicode behavior changes them.

## Out of Scope

- Email delivery of any kind.
- Exporting email, creation timestamps, or any invite fields other than name and phone.
- Real SMS provider credentials, delivery retries, bounce handling, or scheduling.
- Adding invitation links, RSVP tracking, acceptance/rejection states, authentication, or access control.
- Deleting expired invites or automatically purging invite history.
- Building a user interface, file-download endpoint, scheduler, or background job.
- Changing pricing behavior.

## Further Notes

The current codebase already provides a notifier abstraction with SMS and email methods, plus a recording notifier suitable for lifecycle tests. The implementation should preserve that seam while selecting SMS only. The 30-day rule is precise: an invite created at time T is active before T + 30 days and expired at T + 30 days. The current display-name implementation strips non-ASCII characters, which explains the blank Arabic output and should be replaced with Unicode-safe handling. CSV export is intentionally limited to Finance’s name-and-phone requirement.
